subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CONFERENCE RESPECTING SCHOLARSHIPS AND FELLOWSHIPS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the house will recall that at the commonwealth trade and economic conference in Montreal a decision was taken in principle to establish a new scheme of commonwealth scholarships and fellowships. The conference agreed that the exact scope and detailed arrangements for this scheme should be worked out at a further conference of the commonwealth countries to be held in the United Kingdom in 1959. It was also agreed that the mandate of this conference would include a review of existing arrangements for co-operation among commonwealth countries in the field of education to determine the need for any improvement or expansion of these arrangements.
All commonwealth governments including Canada have now accepted an invitation from the United Kingdom government to attend a conference on the lines agreed upon at Montreal, this conference to be held at Oxford, England, from July 15 to July 29. Lord Halifax, the chancellor of the university, has agreed to serve as president of the conference and Sir Philip Morris, the vice chancellor of Bristol University will serve as chairman. The composition of the Canadian delegation to the conference will be decided at a later date.
Meanwhile, the house will wish to know that a meeting is to be held in Ottawa shortly between government officials and representatives of Canadian universities to discuss the arrangements for Canadian participation in this commonwealth scholarship scheme.

REPORT ON MUNICIPAL INCENTIVE PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your permission and that of the house I should like to report briefly on the present status of the municipal incentive program, and to make an announcement. As the house knows, this program was designed to assist in combating seasonal unemployment. As at March 20 I am pleased to report that the number of jobs provided under this program had reached a total of 32,000. That is a total of 32,000 jobs which would not otherwise have been provided.
Those who consulted the dominion bureau of statistics report yesterday will know from that report that this program has played a positive part in the present encouraging increase in employment and the reduction in unemployment which is now taking place. The house may be interested at this time in knowing that since this program was first announced we have received and processed 1,909 applications from municipalities across Canada. Of this number we have approved 1,838 applications or 96 per cent of the total, and a number are still pending. The aim has been, of course, to grant the maximum number of approvals in line with the objective of this program in order to put the maximum number of men to work. The estimated total cost of projects approved to date is $81,375,000.
The federal contribution necessary to launch projects of such magnitude has been slightly more than $9 million; to be exact, $9,279,000. This is the estimated federal share of payroll costs for the period in question from December 1, 1958 to April 30, 1959. The total payroll costs are estimated at $27,358,000. The cost of works to be completed during the period indicated is $52,739,000. Total payroll cost during the period is estimated at $18,706,000. Of this the federal share, as I have pointed out, is a little over $9 million. Thus the federal government's share of direct payroll costs for the period in question represented 17.6 per cent of the total cost of the works for that period.

I mention this, Mr. Speaker, in order to indicate for the benefit of hon. members the extent to which the provinces and the municipalities have co-operated in taking advantage of this program and in making possible works of the magnitude mentioned and, of course, in providing jobs both directly and indirectly to a great many Canadians.
As the house is aware, the success of the program to date has resulted in numerous requests that the period of time be extended. I should add that a number of such requests have come from provinces some of which are contributing to payroll costs in the amount of 25 per cent and 30 per cent, adding a further incentive to the municipalities.
The house will recall that a supplementary estimate was recently approved granting funds in the amount of $15 million for this program. In order that those municipalities which have taken advantage of this program to undertake during the winter months works and projects which they would not have otherwise undertaken, may be enabled to continue to receive this assistance for another full month, I am happy to announce that it is the intention of the government to grant an extension of this program until May 31.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gordon Churchill (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: SALT FISH-STATEMENT BY MINISTER ON MARKETING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on August 1, 1958 I announced the government's decision that the exclusive right to export processed salted fish from Newfoundland, held by the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited, would not be extended beyond July 31, 1959.
By the act of union between Canada and Newfoundland, the exclusive licence to export salted fish, which had been granted to the Newfoundland Associated Fish Exporters Limited by the commission of government, was continued for a period of five years in order to allow the orderly development of alternative marketing arrangements during this period of transition.
At the expiration of the licence arrangement with NAFEL in 1954 it was again agreed to continue the exclusive licence for a further period of three years, with the qualification that interprovincial trade in salt bulk was freed from this restriction. Subsequently two extensions of one marketing year each were granted, the final one at the time of my statement on August 1 last. Thus the salt fish industry of Newfoundland has had a ten-year period in which to adopt marketing methods in conformity with the practice of this trade in other Atlantic provinces and Quebec.
Serious consideration was given to alternative methods of marketing salt fish in Newfoundland. An interdepartmental committee made an extensive and exhaustive survey of the situation. Exporters, processors, fishermen and government officials in the Atlantic provinces and the province of Quebec were interviewed and given an opportunity to present their views.
After full consideration of all aspects of the trade, it was not found possible nor deemed in the best interests of the salt fish industry to adopt alternative methods of controlled marketing in the province of Newfoundland. Accordingly the export marketing of Atlantic coast salted fish after the 31st July, 1959, will be carried out on the basis of free competition.
The government will continue its present practice of supervising the inspection of Atlantic coast salted fish by the Department of Fisheries and will extend to exporters trade promotion assistance through the Department of Trade and Commerce in Canada and our trade commissioner service abroad.

Last year we set a record total of 316 million bushels. Even with the slight decline I have mentioned, our export total should amount to 300 million bushels.
We are in a world situation where exportable surpluses are greater than they were a year ago. At the same time it is expected that world trade in wheat will be higher than it was a year ago, which offsets to some extent the exportable surplus which is being held largely by the United States, Australia and Russia. However, Canada's position in the commercial markets of the world is still as good as it was a year ago. Some of the extra exports from the United States are very likely due to that country's surplus disposal program. In general, Canada's export position with regard to wheat is holding up very well and we shall experience another record year.

speechtext:
I shall deal for a moment with the general history connected with the establishment of the system of parliamentary assistants, the beginnings of which go back to a recommendation contained in a report made on the organization of the public service of Canada in 1912 by Sir George Murray, who was given the responsibility by the then prime minister of Canada, Right Hon. Robert L. Borden. At page 10 the following appears:
Under present conditions there is only one political officer in each department, namely, the minister in charge of it. As a cabinet minister he has work of the highest importance to perform outside his department: and even if the relief which I have above indicated could be afforded to him within his department-
Which consisted of suggestions as to changes that might be made in order to improve the administration of the various departments.
-his parliamentary and other duties would still be a heavy tax on his time, especially in the case of those ministers who are in charge of the more important departments.
Then there was a further reference to the same matter by a special senate committee on the machinery of government in 1919, the chairman of which was the late Senator J. S. McLennan. At page 11 of the report it is stated:
We propose that time be made for these duties-
The reference is to the responsibilities of a minister and his duty to shape policy.
-by the employment of parliamentary undersecretaries as assistants to the ministers. We conceive that their highest usefulness will be found by not circumscribing their duties to occasional replies to a question in parliament, but by
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries making them active and indispensable forces in the working of the departments.
It goes on to set forth the views of that committee, which at the moment I want to make very clear are not necessarily adopted or accepted by the present government. Then you will recall, sir, that in 1936, following the change of government and the return of Right Hon. Mr. King as prime minister, the speech from the throne in that year contained the promise that at the session of 1936 parliamentary secretaryships would be provided.
Well, my hon. friends opposite had a moment of jollity as I commenced. I point out that seven long years passed by before there was any further reference to that subject by the then prime minister or his government. It was not until 1943 that anything further was done in that connection.
It is a matter of interest that there were members supporting the government of that day who were in favour of the establishment of the system. That very distinguished lawyer, A. G. Slaght, who was a member of this house, dealt with the question in 1936, believing that the speech from the throne did indeed reveal the expectation of a hope to be attained. Then on February 12, 1942, as found at page 539 of Hansard, Mr. Slaght put forward in the house a number of names of members of parliament from the government side who would be suitable to act as parliamentary secretaries. As a member of the opposition then I remember the surprise of the present Minister of Public Works and myself at being referred to by Mr. Slaght as potentially qualified parliamentary secretaries. That was in 1942. That was just a step in the direction, according to Mr. Slaght at that time. He said that parliamentary secretaryships or assist-antships constituted a training, as I remember, that ultimately led to the attainment of cabinet rank.
Various other references have been made to the subject, and textbook writers have dealt with it at great length. I simply point out where hon. gentlemen may secure the fullest references. There is the late Mr. Dawson's work, "The Government of Canada." He referred to the subject at length at page 265 and following. I am going to content myself with merely giving one reference, in which he says:
The case for parliamentary assistants is overwhelming. They make possible, through a greater consolidation of departments, a desirable reduction in the number of members in the cabinet; they allow the prime minister to give more equitable and wider representation to various provinces; and they furnish the finest training for young promising members who aspire to cabinet positions.

Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries
Then he refers to the words of Mr. King at the time he introduced the expenditure provided by the estimates with respect to this matter. Without being facetious in any way I must say that I am looking forward to hearing Mr. King's Boswell, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate, give us that knowledge which is peculiarly his respecting this organization and the manner in which it functioned.
Appointments were made, the earliest being made in 1916. The government of Sir Robert Borden made provision for such appointments first under an order in council passed pursuant to the powers contained in the War Measures Act and later by act of parliament. It is interesting to know that among the first named in July, 1916 was Colonel Hugh Clarke, member of parliament for Bruce, who is still alive today and is an outstanding publicist and public spirited man whose devotion to Canada is recognized by all of us without regard to party. Mr. McCurdy was appointed parliamentary secretary for the department of militia and defence, later on resigning and being succeeded by Colonel Clarke who in turn was replaced by F. H. Keefer, M.P.
I am not going to place the orders in council on the record. It was provided, however, that the appointments would be limited to the continuance of the then war, and that appointments might be made from either house of parliament. I think I can do no better than refer to the remarks of Mr. Mackenzie King on this subject. He dealt at very great length with the establishment of the system of parliamentary assistants, and the debates in that connection are to be found in Hansard for April 20 and 21, 1943. The general purpose of the establishment of a system of parliamentary secretaries is to make parliament more effective, to make provision for assistance in many of the phases of a minister's life and thereby lighten the load of responsibility which rests on those who occupy the treasury benches.
Indeed, as one reads the remarks of Mr. Mackenzie King one is impressed by the experience he had as it is revealed in the course of his speech, as well as the speech made by the late Viscount Bennett when the subject came up in the house in 1936, concerning the responsibility that rests on those who are charged with office under our system of democracy.
Our purpose is at all times to improve and strengthen parliament as an institution; to make possible an opportunity for members in various parts of the country to learn of the operations of the departments and to participate in a specialized manner in doing
IMr. Diefenbaker.l

those things which are allotted the departments under statute and as particularly interpreted and applied by the ministers. After all, the major question is to keep parliament in a position of not being unchanged and unchangeable.
I believe in this regard I have the approval of a very profound student of this subject, and I say that with respect, the hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate. We maintain ancient traditions; we change to meet those changes that come about through the complexities of modem government. We change some of the forms, but maintain the mandate. We alter, to meet altering conditions, the techniques of parliament. We do not change the great and abiding things that have remained with us as our legacy from the generations past.
Some years ago changes were made when the rules committee was set up. I viewed those changes in the rules with some doubt before they were presented. After they were presented they represented a step forward and had the unanimous support of members from all sides of the house. I feel there are many other changes we might make, but I do not want to divert in that connection. As I visit other democratic institutions I find, for instance, that in the recording of the vote in India, in the representative parliament of that country, it takes less than a minute and a half whereas in this house it takes from 15 to 25 minutes. After all, I believe those changes are changes of the type that could be considered. They derogate nothing from the dignity of parliament, but they do bring about that saving of time which is necessary so that other matters of greater consequence may receive the fullest consideration.
Now, sir, one of the outstanding works on the subject of the relationship between ministers and parliamentary secretaries is that of the outstanding leader of the Labour party in the United Kingdom, Right Hon. Herbert Morrison. In his book "Government and Parliament", he sets forth on pages 59 and following something of the condition of affairs in the United Kingdom parliament. He says:
Each departmental minister usually has a parliamentary secretary to assist him, but in some of the larger departments there may be two. Mostly, they are members of the House of Commons, or if not, then of the House of Lords. They must not, of course, be confused with the permanent secretary who is the senior civil servant in the department. Nowadays, they are selected by the prime minister in consultation with the minister concerned.
In the United Kingdom, while they are not appointed by the sovereign, the sovereign in every case is entitled to be informed of

the proposed appointment although constitutionally he has no powers. The reason for the system of parliamentary secretaries, as viewed by Mr. Morrison, is that in the main they constitute a help to the ministers and also enable that training to be received that, in some cases, does bring about the attainment of further advance. Assistance is given thereby to the answering of questions and familiarization with public administration.
Those were some of the points mentioned by Mr. King when in 1943 he introduced the measure. He said that one of their purposes is to assist, in general, in any capacity in which the minister may deem advisable; to keep in touch with other members. But, he pointed out, appointment did not mean attachment for all time.
In 1943 Mr. King was asked why it was that a period of time had passed by, a period of seven years. He said he did not know why the appointments were not proceeded with, and he followed that by dealing in general with the difficulties which he, as prime minister, was experiencing, and which prime ministers in general experience. I think in general we are now carrying out what Mr. King had in mind in 1943 when he first introduced the system. A question was asked as to why he proceeded by an item in the estimates rather than a bill, and he gave his answer on April 20, 1943, as reported at page 2380, which was as follows:
That causes me to say a word as to why I am asking the house to vote the necessary supply by an item in the estimates rather than to support a bill setting out more or less in detail the duties and functions of those who are to fill these positions.

Because of the fact that the system is to be embodied in statute form, there will be removed any suggestion that the acceptance of a position as parliamentary assistant is in any way a contravention of the Senate and House of Commons Act, and I hope that general support will be given to it. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, when I view some of the anxious looking faces on the other side I am reminded of that ancient line, "To live by the will of one man is the cause of all our misery." Members of the C.C.F. group support the principle and purpose of this legislation. We, like the Leader of the Opposition, recognize the heavy burden imposed on senior members of the cabinet by their responsibilities under modern conditions and the need for the help of qualified persons to lighten that load, particularly while parliament is in session.
Before proceeding further I wish to thank the Prime Minister for his historical review of the situation from 1912 until this monumental day. I also enjoyed the summary of the history of parliamentary assistants and parliamentary secretaries to which we were treated by the Leader of the Opposition.
In my opinion when the bill is introduced, to be correctly named it should be entitled, "A bill for the relief of the suspense of certain Progressive Conservative members who have been waiting in the wings for over a year;" short title: "An act for the appointment of parliamentary secretaries."
We also endorse the government's decision to provide for the appointment of parliamentary secretaries by an act of parliament rather than continuing the former unsatisfactory, somewhat questionable and piecemeal procedure. When this legislation is passed parliamentary secretaries will be able to accept their remuneration in good conscience and without any fear of criticism in so far as the propriety of the remuneration is concerned inside the house or out.
This apparently unpretentious legislation is of far greater significance than its simple


language would suggest. First of all I must say rarely does a prime minister have occasion to introduce legislation with such interesting implications as this. This must be important legislation because the Prime Minister is piloting it and he attends only to the more important things that happen in this parliament.
This legislation will receive the unanimous approval of all parties in this house and the whole-hearted and fervent support of the Prime Minister's followers although this will be followed later, when the legislation is proclaimed, by the keen disappointment and heart rending of a certain number of the Prime Minister's disciples. I witness the air of expectancy on the government benches, the shining eyes all fixed on the Prime Minister in adoration, supplication and in anticipation. I might say, not only shining eyes but in two cases, dewy eyes.
Soon the Prime Minister, the director of the nation's greatest stage, will have to choose the preferment from the many aspirants among his followers those who are to play supporting roles in the cast of that great drama, the Canadian vision, playing continuously to interested audiences since June 10, 1957.
I cannot resist commenting that with one lightning, legislative stroke the Prime Minister-not understood as yet by hon. members of this house or by the people of Canada, but they will see through it in the future-* has clearly separated the ranks of those who believe in free enterprise into Progressive Conservatives and Liberals. With this measure the Prime Minister casts out the word "assistant" with its plebeian origin, history and meaning. Not for him to be surrounded by persons recognized as underlings and underworkers or known as assistants after the fashion of the smaller retail trades. Instead, the hon. gentleman introduced the word "secretary", derived from the Latin and of ancient usage, meaning according to the dictionary, "a scribe with learning, a confidential officer"; a word replete with Tory, Disraelian, and foreign office tradition and meaning.
In this bill the Prime Minister indicates his disapproval of the language and words used by the former prime minister, Mackenzie King, and his regard for the principles and practice of Disraeli, Balfour and Baldwin. This legislative bow to the great Conservatives, this renunciation of Liberal practice, will cause doubting Tory chests, far and wide, high and low, to breathe a sigh of relief knowing that in the use of the word "secretary" the party has returned to first principles and represents a brand of free enterprise distinct from the wavering and plebeian

course ol Liberalism. This measure demonstrates beyond the shadow of a doubt the deep and unbridgeable gulf between the Progressive Conservatives and the Liberal party.
I shall now turn from a philosophical approach to a microscopical appraisal of this legislation. Parliamentary secretaries can play an important part in parliament. According to my reading on the subject-and I have done a little reading on these questions over the years-they are required to be persons of intelligence, initiative and industry; to be sedate, sedulous and sagacious; to be pleasant, plausible and pleonastic. Their duties and responsibilities have been defined as a result of long experience in the parliament at Westminster.
Although I was a bit flustered at first when I thought the Prime Minister was going to steal my quotes, I confess I was pleased when I saw him refer to that very excellent volume, "Government in Parliament", written by the Right Hon. Herbert Morrison. I congratulate the Prime Minister for going to Labour Party authorities for his material. I wish to quote briefly from this volume because I trust that after the parliamentary secretaries have received their appointments and their anxiety is relieved, to that extent they will use the Hansard of this day as the Canadian encyclopedia for parliamentary secretaries. At page 66 of this book I find the following:
Life of a Parliamentary Secretary
The life of the parliamentary secretary can be interesting and fairly full, or, on the other hand, uninteresting and rather empty according to the attitude of the minister and, to some extent, the higher civil servants. If, departmentally, he is left out in the cold or given little or nothing to do it is, I think, cruel, foolish, and unfair.
We saw some of that in the session of 1957. I continue:
It is cruel because it will develop unhappiness and bitterness in the heart of the parliamentary secretary; it is foolish because the parliamentary secretary of today is a possible minister of the future and it is desirable for him to learn all he can, including the taking of responsibility: it is unfair because, apart from creating a feeling of frustration, it makes a fool of the parliamentary secretary when he hears through other channels of things he ought already to have known about, and is driven to tell inquiring M.P.'s that he is sorry but he knows nothing about it. Nor should it be forgotten that he has important duties to discharge with and for the minister from the treasury bench. Moreover, there is the important consideration that the proper employment of the parliamentary secretary can lighten the burden of the minister.
And we all agree with that. I think that has been mentioned by the Prime Minister
66968-9-139$
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries and by the Leader of the Opposition. I have one more short quotation which is found at page 69, as follows:
There is another possible injustice to parliamentary secretaries, namely, leaving them out of office consultations and conferences. Obviously it is not always right or convenient to have them present, but systematically to leave them out means that they do not know the background of policy decisions. Moreover, even listening to their chief handling such meetings is an experience and an education which may help them if and when they come to shoulder bigger responsibilities. It was my general rule, therefore, to give instructions that the appropriate parliamentary secretary or secretaries should be present at such gatherings, and I would see to it that they had an opportunity of contributing their views, even though they were by no means always accepted. This not only assisted our deliberations and brought them into the inside of things, but helped them to learn the delicate art of the ministerial handling of civil servants. In the end I would give a decision, but, even though it was a decision that some did not want, everybody would go away happier for having had a share in the deliberations.
I think there is a lot of wisdom in that paragraph as written by the Right Hon. Herbert Morrison.
Another thing, Mr. Chairman, in Great Britain parliamentary secretaries are extremely polite to members of the opposition. In that connection and to illustrate the competence of parliamentary secretaries in Great Britain I would quote a model of lucidity, detail and good diction from a question and answer, a question asked of the parliamentary secretary to the minister of works, which is equivalent to our Minister of Public Works in Canada. The question was:
Mr. Hector Hughes asked the parliamentary secretary to the ministry of works, as representing the lord president of the council, if he will instruct the department of scientific and industrial research to collate, with a view to publication, all scientific information obtained by Her Majesty's government from the recent flights round the earth of the Russian satellite and its appendage.
I do this for the benefit of the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton because I suspect he has been practising. The parliamentary secretary replied in this style, and I offer it to the members as a model:
In consultation with the Royal Society a "World Data Centre" has, following on the international geophysical year, already been established at the radio research station of the department of scientific and industrial research. One of the functions of the centre will be to maintain a bibliography of scientific publications relating to observations on the Russian satellites and associated rockets. This is within the executive function of the research council of the D.S.I.R.
I offer this as a model for budding parliamentary secretaries to study. I notice there has been press gallery comment with respect to parliamentary assistants, and on a number of occasions throughout the years I have seen comments made. Apparently they were not
2192	HOUSE OF
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries held In the greatest esteem by some members of the press gallery. I am going to quote one member, that very well-known member of the press gallery, John Bird, who writes about the birds:
The parliamentary assistant among the birds of parliament hill, is the little red-capped chipping sparrow. Every year you may see him proclaiming his territory from the top of a light standard above the terrace. His song is a monotonous, unmusical trill, like an insect's. This he repeats over and over, with "damnable iteration", but small conviction. Like those other assistants, inside the "Big House", he tells his story by rote, with little hope of persuading anybody, since he so obviously lacks authority.
I quote this because I trust that the parliamentary secretaries to be appointed by this legislation will be a more valuable species, playing a more melodious and satisfactory tune.
I am getting along with my few brief remarks, Mr. Chairman, and I wish to say that we in this group want the answers to a number of questions about parliamentary secretaries. I trust the Prime Minister will give us the answers before the debate is concluded.
Will the parliamentary secretaries be given the status of junior ministers, as they are in Great Britain? What will be their standing in the order of precedence for which there is no provision at this time in Canada? I know that one of the presently budding parliamentary secretaries is rather a stickler for etiquette in the form of dress and precedence. Will they be required to wear a top hat and tails on important occasions?
I also want to know whether there is to be some definition of the duties and responsibilities of parliamentary secretaries. In that respect, I mean that members in the opposition are anxious to know clearly what are the duties and responsibilities of parliamentary secretaries and how far they are justified in trespassing on their time, and so on. Then, we want to know whether the appointments are made for a fixed period of time, for a session or for a parliament or in view of the Prime Minister's reference to the constitutional aspects of the question, are they appointed during good behaviour or at pleasure?
The Parliamentary Guide indicates that a number of potential parliamentary secretaries hold directorships. Three are directors of lumber companies; one is a director of an insurance company; one is a director of a telephone company; another is a director of a coal and coke company; another was national director of the Progressive-Conservative party in 1943-1949; and another rising star was president of the young Conservatives of Canada in 1956-1958.
We in this group, Mr. Chairman, insist on the British practice being followed when they
[Mr. Herridge.l

receive their appointments. They must divest themselves of directorships in companies.
I notice also in the ranks of the potential parliamentary secretaries there are a good number of members of the legal profession who are also members of legal firms or partners in legal firms. These gentlemen are in a rather unusual position. They will be making some sacrifice in accepting the appointment-not all but some of them-as parliamentary secretaries, because we all know that no member of the Progressive Conservative party who is a parliamentary secretary would for one moment think of allowing any particular firm of which he is a member to accept any government business. We want to make our position perfectly clear in that respect, and what we expect.
I now come to another matter. As I understand it, strangely enough the parliamentary secretary will properly receive a larger remuneration than a minister without portfolio. How is that matter going to be adjusted in fairness to everyone concerned, and to comply with the procedure in this legislation.
I want to mention one other thing to which we in this group have given some thought. The Prime Minister has not followed the practice of the former government in appointing the government leader in the senate to the cabinet. We consider that that practice had considerable merit. I think I know the Prime Minister fairly well. He is a person who usually takes the middle course. I know that whenever I see him oscillating between two points of view he will stop at six o'clock. We have a recommendation to make in this respect. In view of the new policy of appointing parliamentary secretaries, would it be possible for him to take a middle course and appoint the government leader in the senate as a parliamentary secretary? In fact, he could be the chief parliamentary secretary, a sort of mother hen, as it were, for the newly hatched brood of parliamentary secretaries in the House of Commons. I just throw that out as a suggestion.
I have dealt with some matters that concern us with respect to these appointments and I trust the Prime Minister will be able to give answers to my questions before the debate concludes. However, on behalf of those parliamentary secretaries to come, those unknown faces opposite that will be known to us after the Easter recess, I presume, I wish to quote the comforting words used by the late Right Hon. Ellen Wilkinson who was a member of the labour cabinet in Great Britain, a very fine woman who unfortunately passed away in 1947. She had

a great wealth of common sense, understanding of human nature and a great appreciation of parliamentary practice. When she was dealing on one occasion with the duties, responsibilities, hopes, aspirations and disappointments that follow in the wake of those who become known as parliamentary secretaries, Ellen Wilkinson suggested these beautiful lines from "Indian Love Lyrics" as a dirge for unhappy parliamentary secretaries:
Less than the dust, beneath thy chariot wheel,
Less than the rust, that never stained thy sword,
Less than the trust thou hast in me, my lord,
Even so, am I.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, after the very thorough review we have had of all the possibilities, philosophies and theoretical difficulties in connection with parliamentary secretaries I do not know that I have anything to contribute beyond what I originally intended to say and that is something which has not been covered by the previous two speakers. In effect I wish to offer the Prime Minister what one might call a short list of good prospects from an outside point of view. He will be aware that no member of parliament can make cutting, nasty or slighting references to other members of parliament so this means that all my remarks have to be on the right side of the borderline toward the good, the favourable and the sweet.
I should explain the origin of my making such suggestions by way of a contribution to the debate. When the house met for the first time last year and there were approximately 180 new members, many of them young, eager and full of the vision, 1 think all of us were aware that the whole house seemed to throb with energy and ambition. One of the great features of the House of Commons is that we are not confined within separate party channels. Fortunately we do mix and have our conversations in very many places. All of us get a finger on the pulse of what is going on in the other parties and since there are some 208 people in the government party we have some idea of what is going through their minds and what are the ambitions and feelings of these people.
I know that we are all peers here but as an ordinary member for parliament naturally I am not in touch with the ministers. Nonetheless perhaps I can bring something to this debate for the benefit of the Prime Minister. I do not feel I have the antenna that the Prime Minister perhaps had in getting the feelings of people throughout the country but I suggest that my antenna has been in operation feeling the moods and aspirations
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries and in some sense getting a cross-section of the ability of the potential parliamentary secretaries.
Picking parliamentary secretaries or parliamentary assistants as they were called is all part of what has been going on for a long time in Canada, the organization and selection of the cabinet. The Prime Minister quoted Mr. Dawson who has written the standard work on the government of Canada. Normally a prime minister has to consider when forming a cabinet the factors of geography, region and province. They are very important. You cannot slight one part of the country. He has to look at religious considerations and to a certain extent, I suppose, at ethnic considerations so far as the other major group is concerned. Then, of course, there are always the political considerations. There are such things as shaky seats that perhaps a little bit of a push will help. All these factors come into play.
One of the things I most admired about the Prime Minister when he formed his cabinet was that he did not restrict himself to what many political scientists considered had become the pattern, namely that Quebec had to have five members of the cabinet, four of whom had to be French Canadian Catholics and one an English speaking Protestant; that Ontario had to have a certain number, and that the ministers of public works and justice had to come from Quebec. He more or less threw such considerations aside and left the field fairly wide open. I think anyone who will look at the cabinet as it was first appointed and as it is now will agree that is so. Traditionally, even in the days of the great mentor, Mackenzie King, parliamentary assistants also were usually appointed with these geographical factors in mind but the present Prime Minister again gave us an indication of his range of view and the fact that he would step outside standard procedures.
I have a list here of the 13 parliamentary assistants appointed two years ago and it is very interesting and flattering to me as a member from Ontario that eight of them were from the province of Ontario, true recognition in my opinion of high educational standards and a great amount of ability. There was one from Quebec, one from Alberta, one from New Brunswick, one from Nova Scotia, one from Manitoba, none from Prince Edward Island, none from British Columbia and none from Newfoundland. This seems to me to be an indication that the Prime Minister is going to pick his parliamentary secretaries to quite an extent on the basis of their ability and flair rather than on the basis of strict geographical considerations or other such factors.
The Leader of the Opposition referred to another point that arises with regard to
2194	HOUSE OF
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries parliamentary secretaries, a point about which the Minister of Justice spoke a few years ago, the question of cabinet solidarity. In choosing these parliamentary secretaries the Prime Minister and his colleagues will want to pick people who they feel will fit into cabinet solidarity.
There is also the question referred to by Mr. Morrison, Mr. Dawson, Mr. King and other authorities, the jealousy or fear that may develop when there is an incompetent or relatively incompetent minister and a young, thrusting, ambitious parliamentary secretary. These things indicate that there are hardly any rules that can be laid down as to the relationship between a minister and his parliamentary secretary but there is a need to have parliamentary secretaries who will be affable and who will to a certain extent know their places.
Another factor that is involved is one that the Prime Minister has already mentioned, and that is this question of "young". In parliamentary terms, just what is young? I checked the age of the parliamentary assistants who were appointed two years ago, and while I do not want to go into detail by going through the roster, there are two names on the list whom I have a hard time thinking of as young. I know they are young in spirit, but beyond that one has a hard time thinking of them as young. I know that the legislation will not likely set an age ceiling, but that is one of the factors that have to be considered. In my short list of suggestions, I have tended to concentrate on what I call young people.
One of the other factors, of course, that has not been mentioned at all in the selection of parliamentary secretaries, is that of introducing a woman into these points. Again, the Prime Minister has a very limited choice. He has taken the first step by introducing the first lady into the cabinet, and now he has an opportunity of establishing another first for his government by introducing the first lady parliamentary secretary. Of course, as I said, his choice is limited because there are only two. I would that he had more, but this is a factor that has to be considered.
The hon. member for Kootenay West mentioned another factor and that is parliamentary secretaries for the Senate, that is making some hon. member of that house a parliamentary secretary. I was interested in finding that this topic has already been up for discussion in the other place this session. It was introduced by a member of the opposition and the thought there should be several parliamentary secretaries in that place. However, that is something else.


There is another definite problem in connection with parliamentary secretaries. Last year I was rather shocked when the Prime Minister said he hoped the day would never come when being a member of parliament was a full-time job. A lot of us took that to mean that if we are finding being a member of parliament a full-time job, then there is something wrong with us. I would introduce the question, are these parliamentary secretaries to be full-time jobs or are they just to be sessional? Then, there is the point raised by the Hon. George Drew when he was leader of the opposition, and this is something about which we need information. He raised the point in connection with the rules of the house whether parliamentary assistants have the right to close debates on bills or whether they have the authority to speak for the minister on estimates. This is a point that should be settled.
One of the other aspects of this matter in which we are interested is the number of parliamentary secretaries to be appointed. I have heard a figure of 20 mentioned. If we get the figure up as high as 20, and add to that the number we now have in the cabinet, then you have a type of patronage in the hands of the Prime Minister which could be very powerful. I wonder whether or not that many parliamentary secretaries are necessary? There is a little book written by an independent member of parliament in Great Britain, W. J. Brown, entitled "Guide to Parliament". He said:
In the second place, the scope of government patronage has widely increased of recent years. We have now to deal not only with the eighty paid posts of a ministerial kind, but a large additional number of governmental or quasi-governmental posts which are within the gift of government, which, in filling them, acts largely on the advice of the whips.
He goes on to say that this whole tendency of the ministry, and what attaches to it, is growing and is very dangerous to the point of view of the freedom of the individual member voting as he pleases in certain cases. We are very much aware of the fact that in this particular house very few of us always vote according to our whims, but we tend to follow the party line. There are considerations. For example, the hon. member for York-Scar-borough has a bill coming up upon which I hope we will have a free vote, and that is the bill in connection with capital and corporal punishment. Are parliamentary assistants going to be tied to whatever happens to be the view of their minister or the view of the government? I would suggest that this might be one reason for keeping these appointments to a minimum.

One of the great arguments that Dawson makes in connection with parliamentary assistants is that they will be of assistance to some cabinet ministers. I do not think the Prime Minister touched on this. I quote:
The greater use of members of the house as parliamentary assistants to certain ministers would do much to relieve the work of their seniors, and it would incidentally also make it easier to reduce the number of those in the cabinet proper.
Dawson goes on to make the point that really fisheries does not merit a ministry. I stand corrected, he does not say that fisheries does not merit a ministry but he says fisheries does not merit a post in the cabinet. He says the same thing of the Department of National Revenue and the Post Office Department. We do not know whether or not this is a part of the plan of the Prime Minister in introducing parliamentary secretaries, that is to reduce the size of the cabinet. However, we may suggest that is always an ideal, if it is possible, to keep the executive as small and tightly knit as possible. If this could be done through the introduction of more parliamentary assistants, that would be all to the good.
In the past, in so far as the ministry of fisheries has been concerned, if the minister came from the east coast then the parliamentary assistant came from the west coast. Personally, I wonder whether, with a department of that scope and size, it is necessary to have a parliamentary assistant. On the other hand, when I look at the ministry of transport, which has grown so large and has spread over so many fields, and is going to continue to grow, I wonder whether it would not be possible to have two or three parliamentary assistants for that department, one for air, one for sea and one for land communications. There are a number of departments which, I feel, fall into that category. For example, the Minister of Finance, according to one of the members of the press gallery, hired a young man at $10,000 a year in order to humanize the face the Minister of Finance presents to the public. We would suggest more parliamentary assistants-and again they will be on my short list here- could do a great deal to take some of the pressure off the Minister of Finance in this particular regard.
There is one other point we need to mention in connection with parliamentary assistants, especially when I look at some of them sitting over there, and that is that it is not always certain that you go on from parliamentary assistant to bigger things. We have one gentleman sitting in the house now, the hon. member for Ottawa West, who gave many years of service as a parliamentary assistant and who never achieved any higher post. I know the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries was looked upon, when he became a parliamentary assistant, as a young man in a hurry. Unfortunately, the year 1957 came along and he had nowhere to go.
One of the great things that I envisage may come out of the appointment of these parliamentary secretaries is something that may be more clearly understood if I were to read some remarks by the Right Hon. Winston Churchill. This is what Mr. Churchill said in 1939:
What is the use of sending members to the House of Commons who say just the popular thing of the moment and merely endeavour to give satisfaction to the government whips by cheering loudly every ministerial platitude, and by walking through the lobbies oblivious of the criticisms they hear. People talk about our parliamentary institutions and parliamentary democracy, but if these are to survive it will not be because the constituencies return tame, docile, subservient members, and try to stamp out every form of independent judgment.
The relevance of this particular extract to my remarks is this. I feel that any time you get 208 members together, even though they shelter under the banner of a leader that they revere and under a party of the same name, there is bound to be a breaking out of what one might call rump groups. I think we have looked forward to that in this particular house, the development of a rump group or a ginger group but we have not seen much ginger this session. The point I want to make at this particular time is this. Once these parliamentary secretaries are appointed, I think there will be the development of such a ginger group; that is one of the reasons why we should like to see this legislation pushed through immediately so that out of the bitter need for recognition, some of the disillusioned and disappointed and heartbroken will move to be that rump.

He gave a magnificent performance on the trained seals that flipped on the Liberal backbenches. He said, "They tell us they speak in caucus, but we speak in the House of Commons of Canada where the people of Canada can hear us." I just want to go on from there to one of my members on the short list. I refer to the hon. member for Winnipeg South. During the last campaign in Springfield he was quoted in the Winnipeg Free Press as saying that the Liberals and the C.C.F.'s talk too much in the House of Commons, especially the C.C.F.'s,

Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries and that the Conservative members did their talking in caucus. This raises in my mind a picture of the Wednesday morning caucus being always open to the hon. member for Winnipeg South. I suggest that one of the consequences of appointing him a parliamentary secretary would be that he would be much diminished in the caucus so that there would be opportunities for some of the other hon. members to state their case at that particular time.
One of the parliamentary committees in England a number of years ago looked into this question of parliamentary secretaries and parliamentary private secretaries. I quote from the Journal of the Society of Clerks-at-the-Table in Empire Parliaments:
The parliamentary private secretary has no recognized official position: he acts as the confidential friend and assistant of his minister and necessarily enjoys in very large measure the confidence not only of the minister personally, but of the minister's department and the officials in it. Thus he must necessarily be to some extent imbued with the "team spirit" which is part of the life blood of the ministry; thus, too, his independence as a member of the house must be liable to be impaired to a somewhat greater degree than that of an ordinary member of the party supporting the government in office for the time being, although it would be a great mistake to regard his relations with the government as being as close or intimate as in the case of even the least important under-secretary in the government.
In Great Britain these hybrid personal secretaries are different from the kind contemplated by the legislation the Prime Minister has brought in today. But the comparison that it brings up at the end indicates that the under-secretary, which is the British comparison, has an important position and is definitely related to the ministry. We have no indication of that matter in this particular legislation.
One of the things that Dawson comments on, relating to the former prime minister, Mackenzie King, is this and at page 268 he says:
Yet in the same debate he made the astounding statement that an assistant would have to be persona grata not only to the minister (who is responsible for his actions) but also to the deputy minister (a civil servant), a pronouncement which seemed to justify the unflattering description by one member of the house that the assistants would be nothing more than "official coat-tail bearers" for the ministers.
That brings up the question of whether these parliamentary secretaries are going to have to be persona grata with the deputy ministers according to Mr. King's interpretation. From the minister's remarks I did not catch that he touched on that matter at all. I personally would suggest-and I am sure every other member of the house would go along with me in this regard-that he must be persona grata with the deputy ministers.


The deputy minister has no choice in the matter. However, that is just a question.
If we look at this list of parliamentary assistants for two sessions ago we find that one of the names can be struck out unfortunately because of ill health. I refer to Mr. Angus R. MacDonald. The bearer of one of the positions has gone forward to become Minister of Defence Production, indicating that this is a worth-while channel after all, despite my previous strictures. We are left with these other names, as I said in my interpretation with the exception of two, of young, thrusting, ambitious fellows and, I would think, from looking at the names, men of real ability. What is going to happen to them if they are not appointed parliamentary secretaries this session? I think the inference throughout the whole country will be that they have failed.
Unfortunately we do not know whether or not they have failed. Perhaps it was not their failure at all but rather the minister's failure. I would therefore make a strong plea here to the Prime Minister that he consider on his short list the former parliamentary assistants. I should like to mention especially the hon. member for Saint John-Albert and the hon. member for Carleton. I have had it said to me dozens of times by Conservative members in this house that the hon. member for Carleton deserves to be a cabinet minister. We know that he is kept extremely busy at the present time on the Ottawa scene in his relationship with the government. Perhaps a parliamentary secretaryship would be all that he could handle in lieu of those responsibilities. Perhaps that was the reason that the former parliamentary assistants-

The new company's home office will be in Vancouver, and this is the first time that the home office of a dominion chartered and licensed life insurance company will be located in British Columbia. The owners have indicated their intention of maintaining a substantial investment in the province. Several hundred British Columbia people will find employment with the company as agents and office workers. This is, of course, in line with the present trend of business and gives heart to the statement: "Go West, young man, go west". With a head office in Vancouver, better service can be given to policy holders from that area and it is hoped that other life insurance companies will also construct buildings in the west in order to give similar service.
As I have indicated, if the matter can be referred to a committee for further consideration, I can assure all hon. members that an officer of the company will be present in Ottawa to give any further information required.
