subtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. C-18 to amend the Criminal Code (Capital punishment).
He said: Mr. Speaker, as I was saying last August when I was interrupted by six o'clock, I am sponsoring this bill this session. I must say a word about the activities of other hon. members in this party and in other parties who have spoken in support of this or of a similar bill in the past. I should like to commend them for fighting the good fight over the years on behalf of this proposition. I should like further to make some reference to the many individual citizens groups, civic councils, church and other organizations who have sponsored resolutions and made representations to me and to other members of this and former parliaments on the subject.
Last year in the course of my remarks on this bill I was dealing with the legal system as it exists today and the possibility of tendencies within that system which might prejudice the accused. I dealt with tendencies which might exist in the minds of judges and, at some length, with the tendencies which I knew by personal experience to exist in the minds of certain jurors. I dealt also at that time with the relative abilities of the crown prosecutor versus those of the defence counsel, pointing out that in many cases and, indeed in most cases, the crown prosecutor was a man far more experienced and able in his task than his counterpart engaged in the defence; also that first rate experienced murder defence lawyers did not normally, in spite of the very worthy activities of the legal aid societies, defend most of the murder cases before the courts of this country.
I dealt, further, with the facilities available to the crown and to the crown prosecutor to gather, assemble and document evidence against the accused with virtually
unlimited funds and personnel at their disposal, and compared with this the dilemma of the defence lawyer, particularly when a poor man or a man of modest or no means was accused. How much can a defence lawyer afford to spend out of his own money in these circumstances, with a most unlikely prospect of a fee, if there is to be any at all.
I had meant to refer to some aspects of the present system, particularly with regard to the legal defence of insanity-a defence based on the M'Naghten rule, a precedent for determining insanity in law which has its origin in the year 1843. Several things may be said about this.
The first is that it seems to me that since 1843 few branches of medical science have made such progress as that of psychiatry. When we are dealing with the mind and diseases of the mind surely we must recognize that giant strides have been made since that time although unfortunately these strides are not reflected in the courts and their benefits are not available to juries.
The second difficulty with the law concerning insanity is the position that twelve good men find themselves in when dealing with medical evidence of a psychiatric nature. I wish to quote a statement from a review of a book entitled, "Star Wormwood", by Judge Curtis Bok, of the United States, in which he dealt at some length with this subject. The review states:
Juries should not be required or expected to choose between contesting alienists attempting to apply the prevailing artificial and archaic legal test of insanity. The function of a trial is to find facts, or as Judge Bok puts it, "deeds", or what happened.
I was a member of two juries in which we were concerned with the M'Naghten rule, in both cases hearing eminent psychiatrists supporting different contentions. I confess that all of us were hard put to follow the thread of their arguments and the meanings of the continually changing terms which they applied to support their arguments. These are some of the things that make one wonder if our present processes of law can come to a sufficiently certain conclusion to justify the taking of a man's life.
I should like to quote another reason dealt with in the Canadian Bar Review of May, 1954, in which is contained the record of a symposium dealing with a motion concerning the abolition of capital punishment moved at that time in the name of the hon. member for Parkdale. This reference is from the remarks of one of the participants, Reverend John Kelly, then professor of philosophy at St. Michael's college, University of Toronto.
[Mr. Speaker.!

Concerning one of the aspects of the question I mentioned earlier this afternoon, he had this to say:
The common good also demands that there should be no discrimination against one section of the population. Yet, if the former warden of Sing Sing, Lewis E. Lawes, is to be believed-and I see no reason to doubt his credibility-and if the condition he describes is general-and so far as I can discover there is no reason to suppose that it is not-the death penalty is predominantly and disproportionately imposed upon the poor and upon males. He escorted 150 people to their deaths- 149 were men; 150 were poor. Since the enforcement of the death penalty seems incorrigibly selective, it seems to me that it is working against the common good.
I should like to make reference to the report of the joint committee of the House of Commons and the other place which dealt with capital punishment and reported in 1956 before I proceed to discuss the specific reasons why I am moving this bill. One of the recommendations of that joint committee was as follows:
While the committee considered that capital punishment should be subjected to periodic review by parliament, it recommends that the death penalty should be retained as the mandatory punishment for the crime of murder.
It is in the spirit of that recommendation that I hope we will have a full and comprehensive discussion on this subject at this time representing, if possible, the feelings of all political parties here represented.
The basic arguments for the abolition of capital punishment are several in number and I should like to deal with them in turn, treating some of them rather more extensively than others.
The first suggestion is that it is not actually an effective deterrent. As I mentioned last year there are statistics that can be cited in support of both sides of this question. In the symposium statistics were referred to by Mr. G. Arthur Martin, Q.C., well-known defence counsel of the city of Toronto. With respect to the subject of the death penalty as a deterrent he had this to say:
The state of Michigan, which abolished the death penalty about a hundred years ago, consistently has had a smaller number of murders for each hundred thousand population than its neighbouring states of Ohio, Indiana and Illinois, where it might safely be assumed that conditions of life were comparable. Michigan, however, has a slightly higher incidence of murder than, for instance, Massachusetts or Connecticut, which have retained the death penalty; perhaps the difference is due to cultural conditions, the nature of the population, and so on. On the other hand, Rhode Island, which has abolished the dealth penalty, has a lower incidence of murder than either of its neighbours, Connecticut or Massachusetts, where capital punishment is retained.
When one examines reports, recommendations and discussions on this question over the years one must come to the conclusion
Criminal Code
that a case has not been made that the death penalty is in fact a deterrent to murder.
The second major reason advanced for the abolition of capital punishment is that it is morally wrong. I should like to quote briefly from the report of the joint committee in this regard and leave it at that. At page 12 of the report we find the following:
It was contended that it is morally wrong for the state, as well as an individual, to take human life. The punishment was said to be at variance not only with the principles of Christianity but also with the humanitarian and social developments which characterize the modern world. It was alleged to be an obsolete, barbarous punishment which has been successfully dispensed with in most civilized countries and that it is out of step with modern morality and thought. It was also claimed that the public is revolted by the barbarous nature of the punishment.
I now move on to what has always to my mind seemed the key aspect in the great debate that has ranged on the subject over the years. It is that capital punishment is essentially based on the motive and feeling of revenge. One of the most powerful and compelling statements on this subject appeared in the symposium to which I have made reference. The statement was made by Rabbi Fineberg of the city of Toronto who with respect to his reaction had this to say:
Is any human being exempt from the desire to be appeased by a criminal's contorted agony? I remember the gratification I derived from the hanging of the Nazi war criminals. They had steeped their hands in the blood of six million Jews, the evil they visited on mankind was beyond reckoning-yet I recall my feelings with shame, as unworthy, and as more excusable only in degree than the cries of the mob milling about the gallows at Cornwall prison recently.
My submission is that the motive of revenge is reflected in the fact that capital punishment is not something of which we as Canadians can be very proud. Surely, if motivations for laws exist, in this instance we should be motivated by a desire to protect the public in the determination of our penalties rather than the indulgence of revenge.
On this point, Mr. Speaker, whenever the subject is raised in almost any group, ultimately those who are opposed to the abolition of capital punishment say, "Yes, but what do you mean? What would you do if you caught a man murdering your wife or raping and murdering your child?" My reply to this question, has been as honest as I could make it. It has been that I do not think I or any other man would be held responsible for what he might do when faced with that situation. It is interesting to note that if a man comes across somebody murdering his wife and takes action to prevent that person from murdering his wife I doubt whether the records of the trials in this country or in any

Criminal Code
other country will show many if any convictions under such a set of circumstances. This kind of question, Mr. Speaker, I submit proves the point. I concede freely that I am in no condition to govern my actions, emotionally or in any other way, in such a position and yet those same people want to reflect my feelings at that time in the laws of our land concerning capital punishment.
I recall a conversation which is pretty typical of most people's thinking on this matter, a conversation in which we discussed the academic aspects of the arguments pro and con concerning capital punishment. My friend was in large measure in agreement with me. It happened that on that particular day and at a particular point during our conversation we turned on the news. The shocking news of the rape and murder of a small child was given on the television screen. It was one of those coincidences that seemed to bring into focus our argument. At that time the young daughter of this friend of mine, about the same age as the child who had been murdered, came into the room and my friend who moments before had conceded, on the basis of the rational and calm appraisal of the situation, my argument, changed his mind completely on the basis of association of ideas, I suggest. I have not discussed the matter with him since. I hope he is allowing his calm and serene judgment to govern in this matter, as I think we should with respect to all our laws and certainly with one as important as this.
There is another argument advanced with respect to the abolition of capital punishment and it has to do with the question of morbidity, if there is such a word; that capital punishment has its morbid aspects. I quote from the report in this regard:
It was contended that capital punishment is not only unjust to the murderer and ineffective as a deterrent, but is brutalizing in that it has a bad effect, not only upon prisoners and staff of the institutions where it takes place, but on society at large. It was said that the disproportionate publicity which surrounds a murder trial and an execution reflects the morbid instincts aroused by the death penalty. The shocking scenes which have accompanied some executions were cited in proof of these assertions as to the degenerative influence of capital punishment.
There is a reference in the symposium on this very point, in this connection again by Mr. G. Arthur Martin, Q.C. He had this to say:
I suggest to you, if we are honest with ourselves, that we, as individuals, are in fact ashamed of the retention of capital punishment as part of our penal system. If this is not so, why is the identity of the executioner concealed? Why should his name have to be kept secret so that he will not be shunned by his neighbours? Why is the execution of the death penalty shrouded in secrecy, if it is a deterrent even when secretly carried out?

Actually, if it is such an effective deterrent as its proponents would have us believe, everybody should be encouraged to witness executions-perhaps they should be compelled to witness them-so that they will see to what ends their crimes will lead them if they do not restrain their impulses.
Let me move on to the next and perhaps the most obvious factor in this whole argument, namely the risk of error. The risk of error I submit on the basis of what I have said earlier in this discussion can create the doubts on those lines raised in the public mind by the recent revelations, later denied, in connection with the Coffin case. It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that two members of the Conservative party in this house were on opposite sides of the legal battle which took place in the Coffin case. Something that has always disturbed me about the Coffin case is the fact that at one point the accused had escaped. He was as free a man as one can be when one is a fugitive from justice; but at least he was not in jail. The submission of the defence in that trial, if I recall it correctly, was that when he was approached and found in fact by the lawyer he, in the process of being convinced to return to trial was influenced, I am sure, by the fact that if he was innocent, as he knew in his heart he was, under our system of justice he simply would not be found guilty. I do not know what force in law and in the courts this argument might have; obviously, it was not too powerful an argument.
That left very serious doubts in my mind and in the minds of many of my fellow Canadians. There are other examples. One sent to me by one of the many people who wrote to me following the introduction of this bill earlier this year concerned a prisoner in the United States named James Foster who was under sentence of death for murder. His execution was stayed twice and then convict Charles Rothschild confessed to the killing. I have found myself wondering over the years how many James Fosters in Canada, the United States and other countries have had their time run out on them and how many Charles Rothschilds did not come forward.
I submit that we should remove every possible doubt of the consequences of an error in the trial, that we owe it to society to replace the death penalty with life imprisonment that really means life imprisonment so that in the case of new facts coming to light after the trial has taken place the convicted individual will still be around to be reprieved. I submit that the substitution of life imprisonment that really means life imprisonment for the mandatory sentence of hanging would accomplish the protection of society, as mentioned earlier, and also the protection of the accused.

To continue with the committee report, there is the question of the adverse effect upon the administration of justice, but in this regard there is a reverse effect in the sense that many jurors who have difficulty in coming to grips with the facts in the case and with a quite natural repugnance to being a party to a hanging will reduce a charge of murder to manslaughter. I think any fair person examining the trial records in this country will agree that there have been such cases. As I have submitted, we should be concerned with the protection of society but certainly in this case the result is the reverse in that the charge is reduced in the case of murderers who should be put away for the protection of society and to prevent any future recurrence because of the qualms or squeamishness of jurors, and the sentences of these people are also reduced when they are convicted of manslaughter.
Another reason advanced by the committee has to do with prison administration, and in this regard I should like to quote the report. At page 12 there is the following:
Opponents of the death penalty alleged that the incarceration of all convicted murderers will pose no special problems for prison administration and argued that, as a class, murderers have a superior record to other types of prisoners. Some also urged that, even if the housing of all convicted murderers presented difficulties, it would be improper to permit mere administrative considerations to stand in the way of abolition which was justified on broad grounds of public policy.
These are the conventional reasons advanced on which I and a growing number of Canadians who favour the abolition of the death penalty base our case. My specific purpose in introducing this bill is to change the Criminal Code in such a way that both the protection of society and protection of the accused are preserved.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I know that one should not direct a question to the Speaker but, sir, have you ever seen a man hanged? I have. I saw a young man hanged about 20 years ago because the attorney general of British Columbia told me I did not know anything about abolition or non-abolition of capital punishment unless I had seen a man put to death. It is because of that experience that I say that anyone who has seen the state put a person to death could not help but make a full and comprehensive study of all matters pertaining to the retention or abolition of the death sentence. I have tried to do that over the years, and as a member of the joint committee of the senate and House of Commons on capital and corporal punishment I obtained a great deal of information.
I fully realize that the report of the joint committee contained a recommendation that
Criminal Code
capital punishment be retained but I would draw to the attention of members of the house the fact that so far as the decision of the committee was concerned there was only a difference of three in the vote for retention or abolition, that it was the almost unanimous view of the committee that eventually the death penalty would be abolished and for that reason the committee recommended a review every few years by the house or a committee. It was generally agreed that the only reason why some voted for retention was that they did not think the people of the country were ready yet for abolition.
The evidence is clear, Mr. Speaker. I say it is clear not only from other sources but from the two million words of evidence submitted to the joint committee over a period of three years. You can examine the records of all the countries of the world and the states of the United States and you will find that there is no broad or general differentiation in the rate of homicide between abolitionist or non-abolitionist states or countries.
To those who say that there is protection for police forces in having capital punishment I would point out that prior to 1954 no study had been made of that question whatsoever. The first study ever undertaken in the world so far as we know was undertaken in 1954 by Professor Sellin, one of the world's outstanding penologists. In that year letters were sent to the chiefs of police in all cities of the United States with a population of more than 10,000 asking for information with regard to murders of policemen since the year 1919. When the reports were received they were analysed very carefully and Professor Sellin advised the committee by letter that an analysis of all replies showed there was no justification for the statement that capital punishment was a deterrent to the murder of law enforcement officers.
So, both from the angle of a deterrent and protection, I say that from all the studies of the question I have made there can be no basis for the retention of capital punishment, unless it is admitted that it is retained strictly on the basis of retribution or revenge.
I know that because my name is closely linked with the stand I take in connection with the abolition of capital punishment. Every time there is a vicious, brutal murder, especially a sex murder, anywhere in Canada, I receive some letters. Sometimes I get quite a few. Almost every one of them says exactly what was pointed out by the mover of this bill, suppose it had been your wife or your mother or your daughter? The point is that the very position these people take is conclusive evidence of the failure of their own argument because the murder took place. We

Criminal Code
have capital punishment, and we have always had capital punishment in Canada.
The records are clear that in most instances when a person kills he does so from an emotion, from a fear, from an attempt to escape from passions; that is something that having capital punishment on the books is not going to deter. I am going to conclude my remarks because my views on this subject are very well known. I did want to say these few words and to add my hope that the endeavours that have been made in the past, together with this new endeavour by the mover of this bill, will have some effect and we will get what start we can upon this modern approach to this very important phase of penology. I hope the day is not too far away when this country will join the majority of other countries in the western world in which this ancient system of revenge has been abolished and where society is protected through the medium of a prison and not through the exercise by the state of a right which the state says is illegal and immoral if followed by the individual.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
It is indeed a pleasure to speak in support of the position taken by the two hon. members who have preceded me in connection with the deterrent value of capital punishment. A little over a hundred years ago capital punishment was the penalty for some 280 offences in England. When it was sought to abolish this penalty there was great agitation amongst the people who feared that might lead to an increase in crime and petty thievery because, at that time, hanging was the punishment for stealing even a sheep. Since that time England has taken the lead and capital punishment has been completely abolished there. I feel it is high time we followed that example.
There is one other point I should like to mention this afternoon. Having had the experience of defending people accused of murder, as I know many hon. members have had the same experience, I can truthfully say that I believe too much depends upon the ability of the lawyer as to whether or not the man is going to be hanged. The life of a man is placed on too precarious a pedestal because so much depends on the feelings of the jury. I feel it is high time that this government took the initiative by following the course advocated in this bill. I am sure that the abolition of capital punishment has the approval of every hon. member in this house.
Certainly the points brought out by both hon. members concerning the immorality of capital punishment should give each and every one of us food for thought. I am often reminded, Mr. Speaker, of the words of

Marshall Hall who made it very clear that, according to the principles of British justice, it is better for a thousand guilty men to go free than for one innocent man to be hanged. How often have we had occasion to think about the Coffin case to which reference was made this afternoon? How often do we think that at times there must be mistakes? It is impossible for lawyers and juries to go on in an infallible manner. I can recall sitting in this house in the opposition on the night that Coffin was to hang. I wanted to rise and ask the cabinet of that day to reconsider the matter because they only had about three hours in which to do so. However, the rules of the house prevented that.
I can recall the feelings I had at that time, and thinking that here was an example of a man who was probably going to the gallows for a crime he did not commit. I can recall thinking that the only means of removing this fear from the minds of Canadians was to abolish capital punishment, once and for all. I think it has been clearly demonstrated here his afternoon that as a deterrent to crime capital punishment does not serve a useful purpose. Recent judicial decisions in the United States are bringing out very clearly the mental aspects that surround these crimes of homicide. The old rule in the M'Naghten case no longer applies in the courts in some states of the United States. They are taking into account the various aspects of mental illness, aspects which have only become known in recent years.
There is one more reason why capital punishment should be abolished, and I feel I would be very grateful indeed if this government were to take the initiative by introducing the necessary measure into this house to abolish capital punishment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT RESTRICTING CAPITAL PUNISHMENT TO CERTAIN OFFENCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, mention has been made in this debate of the joint committee which was formed in 1953 to study the whole problem of capital punishment. I was a member of that committee for a short time toward the end of the sittings. The committee sat for almost three years and they heard witnesses from all spheres of life, lawyers, doctors, psychiatrists, police officers and prison officials. All the arguments were put forward. I think, within my experience, it was one of the most soul-searching committees I have ever seen functioning. Everybody was so anxious to form an honest opinion on the subject.
There were some hon. members on the committee who argued that the retention of capital punishment was a deterrent and that it was a just punishment for murder; that it indicated society's revulsion to the greatest

of all crimes, the taking of life. There was also a basic belief that public opinion was substantially in favour of capital punishment. I think, to a certain extent, that was true. Actually, public opinion is changing a great deal and perhaps the committee had something to do with that change. Gallup polls have been taken on this subject since 1943. In 1943, 73 per cent of the people polled believed that capital punishment should be retained; in 1953 that figure had only dropped to 71 per cent. Seventy-one per cent said it should be retained and 22 per cent said it should be abolished and seven per cent were undecided. But by 1958 there had been a change in public opinion. Fifty-two per cent were for the retention of capital punishment; 33 per cent were for its abolition; and 15 per cent were undecided. As a member of that committee, I think the one factor that influenced my thinking was the claim made by responsible and authoritative people that it was a deterrent to murder. In the final report brought out by the committee on the retention or abolition of capital punishment this statement was made:
The committee was impressed by the virtually unanimous support of the death penalty by provincial attorneys and other provincial law officers and provincial police officers who had responsibility for and firsthand experience in law enforcement in Canadian provinces. These officials without exception testified that capital punishment was an effective deterrent to murder. They considered that it was particularly effective in deterring the professional criminals from carrying weapons and committing crimes of violence. They contended in addition that abolition of capital punishment would endanger police because a criminal seeking to avoid arrest would have much less fear of the consequences of the use of firearms or violence if capital punishment were abolished.
On the basis of this summary and after much soul searching on my part, I was one of those on the committee who voted for the retention of capital punishment. But my soul searching did not stop there. Since 1956 I have done a great deal of studying on the subject. I have read the opinions of people who are far more qualified than am I to form opinions and I have interviewed many experts including judges, lawyers, prison authorities, social and welfare workers and police reporters, and I must confess that I have changed my mind with regard to capital punishment. Although I still believe that it is a deterrent, I no longer feel that that fact overrides more important factors against capital punishment. In listing some of these factors, may I mention the following.
First there is the fact that a considerable portion of murders are undoubtedly committed in sudden and uncontrollable passions and I do not believe that the thought of death in any way would stop those murders.
Criminal Code
I believe the most effective deterrent would be, as the hon. member for York-Scarborough (Mr. McGee) said, life-long imprisonment, really life imprisonment; and even more important, the sure knowledge that they will be detected and apprehended and that they face life imprisonment which to me seems to be a much more severe punishment than the painless form of death.
There is no doubt about the fact that many murderers must be mentally ill and emotionally irresponsible. I do not believe that any normal, sane, law-abiding people should be obliged to assume the responsibility of meting out death to such people. I have had many judges tell me that murder juries are hesitating to acknowledge that the crime is murder and the result is that although the evidence is patently against the accused, juries with the slightest shadow of doubt will bend over backwards and in many cases guilty persons go absolutely free. I think this is another argument against capital punishment.
The one strongest argument undoubtedly is that it is morally wrong for a man to take the life of another man, or for the state to take the life of a man. Like most hon. members in this house I am sure that I have received hundreds of briefs and representations from all kinds of organizations-including church organizations and welfare organizations-and individuals pointing out that capital punishment is not only an obsolete and barbarous punishment but that it is un-Christian and out of step with modern morality. One brief from the Quakers asserted that the wide publicity given to murders tends to make the thought of murder familiar and, to morbid minds, even attractive.
Mr. Speaker, these are just a few of the basic facts which have influenced my thinking with regard to capital punishment. The strongest argument for its retention is that it may be a deterrent to further murders. But I believe the arguments for its abolition are even stronger; and the strongest of all, to my mind, is that undoubtedly it is morally wrong to take a life that God has created.

Mr. Chairman, I have only a few minutes left, and one of the points I wanted to make in connection with this subject is occasioned by the fact that the Prime Minister has made remarks in this house to the effect that he does not care for lobbies, and I would ask him to ignore the lobby in the form of the telegram he received on the night of the last election from a certain member who was a parliamentary assistant, some of whose followers I understand comported a lobby in the form of a telegram to the Prime Minister. One of the points one finds so intriguing is in connection with Prince Edward Island. I, as a teacher, would like to see a fellow teacher, the hon. member from Queens given an opportunity, but we are up against the fact that this is a small province. In so far as

the province of Ontario is concerned, the Prime Minister has two former provincial cabinet ministers available for selection. They foresook the provincial field for higher things in order to support the party, and one would imagine that they will receive serious consideration.
As one moves west, one encounters the hon. member for Athabasca who, as a former police officer, would make a real contribution as parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Justice. The former member of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police was retired from the R.C.M.P. under treasury board minute 527514 dated February 6, 1958 which authorized his retirement from the service under section 97, paragraph (d) subsection 2, which states that one may be compulsorily retired from the force in order "to promote economy and efficiency". He certainly, because of his very forthright nature should be one of those to be considered. The final point I want to make in connection with personnel touches on two members who, from the back benches, have given touching demonstrations of feeling and devotion for members of the cabinet and other leading Conservatives. The other hon. member I would refer to is the hon. member for Joliette-L'Assomption-Montcalm who must surely deserve something because of the devotion he holds for you, Mr. Chairman, hon. member for Longueil.

It depends on how competently the business of this parliament is done, and how much leisure I can get to work on the book. There is really only one observation I want to make about this resolution and it is one which ought to receive consideration from two angles. One is, of course, the protection of the public purse. The other-and this is a more important angle still-is the protection of the independence of parliament.
All hon. members will recall that the first United Kingdom prime minister who was known by the title of prime minister- which was at that time considered to be not a title of honour but a term of opprobrium-said, or is supposed to have said, that every man has his price. I would be the last to hold any such view, and my experience in Ottawa goes back over 20 years. I believe that if the generality of the population had the same high standards of conduct as most public men have, the public would not be the poorer for it. There is, none the less, a danger. We are all human. We are all fallible and we are all subject to many temptations. It may be that very often the temptation of place is more important than the temptation of remuneration, but it is a very healthy rule that no member of parliament and certainly no member of this place should accept any emolument of any kind under the crown unless parliament itself has so decided.
There has, I think, been a regrettable, indeed, a deplorable tendency in some other legislatures-I will not go beyond that-to proliferate offices under the crown in some cases almost to the point where almost half the membership is in receipt of something more than the indemnity of a member. I think that is a very unhealthy situation. I am a practical politician-

-or at least I think I am, and I am no great believer in that kind of independent member who gets up and tries to make a good fellow of himself in the eyes of his constituents by a display of independence of his party simply for the sake of getting his name in the newspapers. There have not been very many men of this sort in our public life and I think, myself, that if we are going to have a party
Provision for Parliamentary Secretaries system and relatively stable government and some resistance to pressures of every kind that come upon every parliament, that in the main the place where the hon. member for Winnipeg South is supposed to have said that independence should be shown is the most effective place to show it.
What I do think is very important is that no matter who is in office and no matter what the government may be there should be in the ranks of the supporters of that government enough people who are both genuinely independent and capable of remaining independent. It seems to me that independence and party loyalty are not in the least incompatible and that it is very important to preserve both.
The Prime Minister will recall that Sir John A. Macdonald is supposed to have said that he had no use for parliamentary supporters who were willing to support him only when he was right. The men he liked were those who would support him when he was wrong. I suspect that the Prime Minister will be as much in need of that kind of support as any other leader we have had. The point I am trying to make is that there should not be slavish support nor the kind that comes from any hopes or expectations of profit, advantage or place. For that reason I sincerely hope that the highly salutary provision that was put in the estimates in 1943 will be included in the bill; that is to say that there should be an upper limit to the number of parliamentary secretaries who may be appointed.
I recognize that there is quite a strong argument that may be advanced to the effect that the government may not know from time to time how many of these secretaries it is desirable to have. However, I suggest that recent experiences in this parliament in this very session illustrate what a salutary thing it is for a government to have to come back to parliament and ask for any additional expenditures. I believe hon. members will understand to what I am referring without my elaborating further.
It seems to me the government should take the responsibility for deciding that any reasonable number of these parliamentary secretaries should be appointed and no more, and I believe 14 would be quite enough. I do not know what the Prime Minister's views are about whether any of these could be appointed in the other place. I do not know if the legislation envisages that. There are certain portfolios that are very onerous. All ministers are equal, we recognize,

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING REDUCTION OF CLASS AND COMMODITY RATES
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, by its decision dated November 17 last the board of transport commissioners, pursuant to the application of the railway association of Canada and certain of the member companies, authorized a general increase of 17 per cent in the class and commodity rates which are noncompetitive, including rates by joint rail-water routes which are differentially related to the rail rates, accessorial services, and specific increases of 22 cents per ton on coal and coke. No increases were authorized for statutory rates on grain and grain products, import and export related rates, and international rates between the United States and Canada; nor did the board authorize increases in competitive rates, in as much as the making of such rates is within the discretion of the railways, and is governed by the exigencies of competition.
The decision of the board was appealed by eight provinces to the governor in council, and while the governor in council recognized the need of the railways for the additional revenues which would thereby be obtained, and did not disallow the increase, it was the view of the government that a means of granting some relief from the increase should be devised.
As an interim measure designed to alleviate the burden of the authorized increase in rates, the proposed legislation provides for a subsidy of $20 million over a 12-month period, to be paid to the companies that are subject to the board's order No. 96300 as reimbursement for such reductions in rates as they may be directed to make pursuant to this legislation. The companies that are subject to order No. 96300, and thereby come within the scope of this legislation, are principally the Canadian National Railways, the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and its leased lines, and a number of smaller railway companies which are member lines of the railway association of Canada; and the water carriers who participate in joint water-rail, and rail-water-rail routes, that is the Canadian Steamship Lines, Northwest Steamship Company and Canadian Pacific Great Lakes Steamships.
The government has decided that the most effective relief is to be afforded by confining the subsidy to a reduction in the noncompetitive class and commodity rates, including the joint rail-water rates which are

Freight Rates
differentially related to the rail rates. These rates are generally known as "normal" rates, and are the ones which have taken the full percentage increases authorized by the board over many years.
This manner of alleviation concentrates the benefits on the long haul traffic where rates have not been kept down by competition. The subsidy will not apply toward a reduction in the other rate categories which I have referred to, whether or not they were authorized to be increased under the board's order.
The legislation provides that the board shall require the companies to reduce their class and commodity rates by such amounts as to effect a reduction in their revenues obtained from this traffic by $20 million during a 12-month period. The exact reduction in rates which will thereby result is a matter which will depend upon traffic volume and not one which the government, by legislation, could fix in advance. I may say, however, that on the basis of the present volume and pattern of traffic it has been estimated that the application of the $20 million subsidy on the basis which I have outlined will permit a reduction of some seven percentage points, thereby making the authorized increase approximately 10 per cent in lieu of 17 per cent.
As hon. members know, the government has indicated its intention of proceeding with a comprehensive inquiry into matters affecting the railways. The proposed legislation therefore limits the assistance to a 12-month period, when it is hoped a report will be available to the government. Consideration will then be given to means of further relieving the unfair discriminatory burden of the freight rate structure.

speechtext: I might answer the hon. member for Laurier on that point now, Mr. Chairman. I thank the minister for that reply. I take it that the long term inquiry he has in mind is one which will cover the whole matter of railway policy as well as the railway freight rate structure. While I do not wish to anticipate what the form of that announcement will be I take it from what the minister has said that it will be a commission of some sort. I am not particularly concerned at the moment whether it be a royal commission or another type of investigation but I am very much concerned with the fact that according to the statement the minister has made there will be a complete investigation into the railway policy of Canada as well as the inequalities, inequities or discriminations which may exist and have existed for some time in the freight rate structure. I wanted to get that assurance from the minister because I intend to come back to that point at a later time.
The matter under discussion this evening is a resolution moved by the Minister oi Transport which divides itself into two parts, The first part is expressed in these words:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to direct the board of transport commissioners to require by order the reduction of class and commodity freight rates (other than competitive rates) charged by carriers subject to the order of the board dated November 17, 1958-

That is the judgment referred to by the minister earlier. The second part is expressed in these words:
-and to authorize payments to reimburse carriers for the resulting reduction of their revenues up to an aggregate amount of $20 million.
The terms of this resolution give rise to a number of questions and it seems advisable to consider these as one proceeds to discuss the statement the minister has made as well as the order of the board. I should like to deal first of all with the judgment and order of the board of transport commissioners which is dated November 17, 1958. The decision, in its recital of the facts on pages 5 to 7, indicates, particularly at page 6, what the railways had in mind.
